claims.text: HfNbTaTiZr is an equiatomic refractory high-entropy alloy.
Vacuum sintering HfNbTaTiZr at about 1400 °C can produce a nearly fully densified alloy.
The vacuum-sintered HfNbTaTiZr alloy is a random solid solution.
Controlled slow cooling or heat treatment promotes nanoscale SRO precipitates in HfNbTaTiZr.
Slow cooling can be applied after sintering HfNbTaTiZr at about 1400 °C.
The proposed cooling schedule provides sufficient time to form nanoscale SRO precipitates without excessive coarsening.
The resulting nanoscale SRO precipitates are uniformly dispersed throughout the HfNbTaTiZr matrix.
SRO precipitates act as phonon-scattering centers.
Scattering by SRO precipitates reduces the phonon scattering time.
Enhanced phonon scattering by SRO precipitates lowers lattice thermal conductivity.
Slow-cooled HfNbTaTiZr containing SRO precipitates will have lower lattice thermal conductivity than an otherwise identical rapidly quenched sample.
Rapid quenching maintains a random HfNbTaTiZr solid solution with minimal SRO precipitation.
The conductivity-reduction effect persists when SRO precipitates remain nanoscale and uniformly distributed.
Precipitate coarsening or macroscopic phase separation compromises the proposed phonon-scattering mechanism.
The magnitude of the thermal-conductivity reduction depends on precipitate size, volume fraction, and spatial distribution.
The experiment compares rapid-quenching and controlled-slow-cooling treatments while holding composition, sintering, and densification constant.
TEM is used to determine precipitate size, distribution, and density.
Failure to observe a statistically significant conductivity reduction despite increased nanoscale SRO precipitate density falsifies the hypothesis.
